title: Mechanistic Interpretability
summary: Circuits, features, superposition, sparse autoencoders, the reverse-engineering-a-neural-network research program.
html:
Every technique in sections 8 through 12 evaluates a model from the outside: give it inputs, observe outputs, score the result. Section 10.8's Sleeper Agents result is the sharpest statement of why that is not enough — behavioral safety training can hide a behavior rather than remove it, and no amount of output inspection distinguishes the two. Mechanistic interpretability is the research program that responds by opening the model up.

The goal, stated as its practitioners state it: reverse-engineer the algorithms a network learned into human-understandable components, with a causal account of how those components produce the behavior. The emphasis on causal and algorithmic is the whole distinction. "This neuron activates on Python code" is a correlational observation. "These attention heads copy the token following a previous occurrence of the current token, and ablating them destroys in-context repetition" is a mechanism — it says what the computation is, and it makes predictions that can be falsified by intervention.

The analogy the field uses is decompilation. A trained network is compiled artifact: the weights implement algorithms, but in a representation nobody designed for reading. Mech interp attempts to recover source-level structure from the binary, without access to source, documentation, or any guarantee that human-legible structure is there to find.

Features and Circuits

Two abstractions carry the whole program, and they came from vision before transformers. Olah and colleagues' Circuits thread (2020, in Distill), starting with Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits, laid out three claims about InceptionV1 that transferred directly:

  • Features are the fundamental unit. A feature is a direction in activation space corresponding to a property of the input — a curve at a particular orientation, a dog snout, a token being a specific person's name, code being inside a string literal. The load-bearing word is direction, not neuron: 13.3 explains why those are not the same thing and why conflating them was the field's central early mistake.
  • Features are connected by weights into circuits. A circuit is a subgraph of the network — specific features, specific connecting weights — implementing an identifiable computation. The vision work traced curve detectors composing into circle detectors, and documented high-low frequency detectors and car detectors assembled from wheel and window features at specific positions. These were verified by reading weights, not by pattern-matching activations.
  • Universality. Analogous features and circuits recur across architectures and training runs — curve detectors appear in many vision models — suggesting some learned structure is determined by the data and task rather than by initialization. Universality is a well-supported empirical tendency, not a law; counterexamples and partial failures exist.

The transformer-specific program was set out in Elhage et al. (2021), A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits (Anthropic), which gave the algebraic decomposition the rest of this section relies on. Its central move: analyze attention-only transformers exactly, decomposing the computation into paths through the residual stream, and identify which weight products actually matter.

The Residual Stream as a Communication Channel

The single most important reframing for reading interpretability work: do not think of a transformer as a stack of layers transforming a hidden state. Think of it as a shared memory bus that components read from and write to.

The architecture makes this exact. Each block adds its output to the residual stream rather than replacing it:

x_0     = embed(tokens)
x_{l+1} = x_l + Attn_l(LN(x_l)) + MLP_l(LN(x_l))
logits  = Unembed(LN(x_L))

Unroll it, and every layer's contribution is a separate additive term:

logits = Unembed( LN( embed + sum_l Attn_l + sum_l MLP_l ) )

Three consequences do most of the work in practice:

  • The stream is a sum, so contributions are separable. You can ask what a single head contributed to the final logits, because its contribution is a term in a sum rather than being entangled through a nonlinearity. This is what makes direct logit attribution — decomposing the output logits into per-component contributions — possible at all.
  • Components communicate through subspaces. Nothing forces a head to read what the previous layer wrote. A head's W_Q, W_K, W_V project the stream down to a low-rank subspace; its W_O writes back into another. Two components communicate when the write subspace of one overlaps the read subspace of another, which sets up the virtual weights picture: the effective connection between two components is the product of the writer's output matrix and the reader's input matrix, even if they are many layers apart.
  • The residual stream is bandwidth-limited and heavily shared. It has d_model dimensions and many more things to carry, so components must pack information into partially overlapping directions. This is the same pressure that produces superposition (13.3), and it is why the stream's basis directions are not individually meaningful.

The framework paper also identified the useful factorization of attention into two circuits per head. This is the vocabulary you will hit constantly:

QK circuit:  W_Q^T W_K   (as a d_model x d_model bilinear form)
             decides WHERE to attend -- which source position
             each destination position reads from

OV circuit:  W_O W_V     (as a d_model x d_model map)
             decides WHAT is moved -- how the attended position's
             content is transformed and written back

The head's action factorizes:
    attention pattern (from QK) x value transformation (from OV)

The framework also distinguishes composition types by which part of a later head a previous head writes into: Q-composition (affecting where it looks via queries), K-composition (via keys), and V-composition (affecting what it moves). Induction heads (13.4) are the canonical instance of K-composition — and note that this multi-head interaction is why a one-layer attention-only model cannot form them.

The residual stream view. Attention heads and MLPs are not sequential transformations of a hidden state; they read subspaces of a shared additive stream and write into it. A circuit is a path through this bus, and two components interact only insofar as one's write subspace overlaps the other's read subspace.

Superposition and Polysemanticity

Early interpretability hoped neurons would be the unit of analysis. They are not, and the reason is now well understood in toy settings.

The observation. Individual neurons are polysemantic — a single neuron fires on unrelated concepts. This is not rare; it is typical. It blocked neuron-level interpretation for years and was widely treated as evidence that networks are simply messy.

The explanation. Elhage et al. (2022), Toy Models of Superposition (Anthropic), gave a compelling account. A model needs to represent far more features than it has dimensions. In n dimensions there are only n mutually orthogonal directions — but there are exponentially many almost-orthogonal ones (the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma is the formal version). If features are sparse — any given input activates only a few of them — the network can assign each feature its own non-orthogonal direction and tolerate the interference, because collisions are rare. Superposition is the network trading a small, mostly-avoidable interference cost for a large gain in representable features.

Setup: represent m features in n dimensions, m >> n.

    x (m-dim, sparse)  --W-->  h (n-dim)  --W^T, ReLU-->  x' (m-dim)

Sweep feature sparsity S and observe the learned W:

    S low  (features usually active)
        -> no superposition. The model keeps the top-n most
           important features orthogonally and DROPS the rest.

    S high (features rarely active)
        -> superposition. m > n features get non-orthogonal
           directions; interference is real but rarely triggered,
           and the expected loss is lower than dropping features.

Observed structure: features organize into geometric configurations
(antipodal pairs, triangles, pentagons, tetrahedra -- tied to
uniform polytopes), and the transition between regimes is not smooth
but shows phase-change behavior.

Why this reframes everything downstream. Polysemanticity stops being a mystery and becomes a prediction: if features live in non-orthogonal directions that outnumber the dimensions, the standard basis directions — the neurons — are arbitrary linear combinations of many features. A neuron looks polysemantic because it is a projection onto an accidental direction. The corollary is the field's key methodological turn: the right object to look for is a direction in activation space, not a neuron, and finding those directions requires solving a decomposition problem rather than reading off coordinates.

Epistemic status, stated plainly. The superposition hypothesis is well-demonstrated in toy models constructed to exhibit it. That is the paper's own framing. The evidence that real language models use superposition the same way is indirect: polysemantic neurons are ubiquitous, feature counts plainly exceed dimension counts, and the SAE results in 13.5 are consistent with the hypothesis. Consistent with is not the same as demonstrated. Treat superposition as the field's best-supported working model, with the toy-model caveat attached.

Induction Heads: The Canonical Circuit

Induction heads are the field's flagship result — a circuit that was found, reverse-engineered, verified causally, and connected to a macroscopic capability. Olsson et al. (2022), In-context Learning and Induction Heads (Anthropic), building on the 2021 framework paper.

The algorithm. Given a sequence containing [A][B] earlier and [A] again at the current position, predict [B]. Prefix matching, then copying — the fuzzy, learned version of a hash-table lookup over the context.

Context:   ... [A] [B] ......... [A] <- current position
Predict:                              [B]

Two heads in two different layers, composed:

  Layer L:   PREVIOUS-TOKEN HEAD
             at each position, attend to position-1 and write
             the previous token's identity into a subspace of
             the residual stream.
             Now position i's stream carries "I am preceded by t_{i-1}".

  Layer L+k: INDUCTION HEAD
             query = current token [A]
             key   = the PREVIOUS-TOKEN info written by layer L
             -> attends to the position whose PREDECESSOR was [A],
                i.e. the position holding [B]
             OV circuit copies [B] into the output direction.

This is K-COMPOSITION: head 1's output enters head 2's KEYS.
It requires at least two attention layers -- which is exactly
what the empirical formation data shows.

Why this result carries so much weight. Four independent lines of evidence, which together are far stronger than any one:

  • The mechanism was read off the weights, not inferred from activation patterns. The QK and OV circuits do what the algorithm says.
  • A visible phase change. Induction heads form abruptly during training, in a narrow window, accompanied by a bump in the loss curve — a small region where the loss deviates from its otherwise smooth power law. A macroscopic training-curve anomaly with an identified microscopic cause is a rare and strong result.
  • The formation coincides with a jump in in-context learning ability, measured as the improvement in loss on late tokens versus early tokens in a context. The circuit appears and the capability appears in the same window.
  • Causal and generalization evidence. Ablating induction heads damages in-context learning. And the heads do more than literal copying: they participate in fuzzier pattern completion, including translation-like and analogical patterns, indicating a general in-context pattern-matching mechanism rather than a string-copy special case.

The honest boundary. Olsson et al. argue induction heads are a major mechanism for in-context learning, with the strongest evidence in small attention-only models and correspondingly weaker evidence in large models. The claim is not that induction heads are all of in-context learning in a frontier model. It is that they are a real, verified, causally-implicated mechanism — and, as of the early-2025 literature, the clearest existence proof that learned algorithms can be recovered from weights.

Sparse Autoencoders

If features are directions and superposition means there are more of them than dimensions, then finding features is a dictionary learning problem: decompose activation vectors into a sparse combination of elements from an overcomplete dictionary. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are the leading approach.

Given activation x in R^d (a residual stream vector, or MLP activations):

    f = ReLU( W_enc (x - b_dec) + b_enc )       f in R^{d_sae}, d_sae >> d
    x_hat = W_dec f + b_dec

    L = || x - x_hat ||^2   +   lambda * ||f||_1
        ____ reconstruct ___/     ___ sparsity ___/

Dictionary is OVERCOMPLETE: d_sae is typically 8x to 100x+ larger than d.
Columns of W_dec are the learned feature DIRECTIONS; entries of f are
the per-example feature activations. The L1 term forces each input to be
explained by a handful of features -- the operationalization of the
sparse, over-complete, non-orthogonal picture from 13.3.

Common variants: TopK SAEs (enforce exactly k active features, removing
lambda-tuning and L1 shrinkage), gated SAEs (separate the decision to
activate from the magnitude), JumpReLU SAEs (thresholded activation).

The empirical results. Bricken et al. (2023), Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning (Anthropic), applied this to a one-layer transformer's MLP activations and found features that were dramatically more interpretable than neurons — responding to specific, describable contexts (particular sorts of DNA sequences, tokens in specific syntactic roles, particular languages) rather than the grab-bag mixtures neurons respond to. Critically, they validated causally as well as by inspection: intervening on a feature changed downstream behavior in the way the feature's interpretation predicted, so this was not just relabeling correlations.

Templeton et al. (2024), Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet (Anthropic), scaled it to a production frontier model — the result that made SAEs the field's central tool. Findings worth knowing precisely:

  • Millions of features extracted from the residual stream of a deployed model, many corresponding to abstract and multilingual concepts rather than surface tokens — a feature fires for a concept whether it is expressed in English, in another language, or in an image.
  • Features form a geometry: nearby directions correspond to related concepts, giving a navigable structure rather than an unordered list.
  • Safety-relevant features exist — features related to security vulnerabilities in code, to deception and power-seeking, to bias — which is the concrete reason interpretability and alignment converge here.
  • Steering works. Clamping a feature to a high value produces the corresponding behavior change, which is causal evidence that the features are used by the model rather than merely decodable from it. The widely-circulated demonstration was clamping a Golden Gate Bridge feature and observing the model's identity and outputs shift accordingly.

Limitations, stated as the field states them. These are active problems as of the early-2025 literature, not minor caveats:

ProblemWhat it isWhy it matters
Feature splittingIncreasing dictionary size splits one feature into several finer variants. A generic "legal language" feature becomes many specific onesThere is no natural stopping point and no principled way to pick d_sae. The number of features you find is partly a hyperparameter, which is uncomfortable for a method claiming to recover the model's actual units
Dead featuresA substantial fraction of dictionary elements never activate on any input and contribute nothingWastes capacity and suggests the optimization is not finding the best decomposition. Mitigated with resampling and architectural fixes, not eliminated
Reconstruction-sparsity tradeofflambda trades reconstruction fidelity against sparsity. Sparser dictionaries are more interpretable and reconstruct worseThe unexplained variance may contain exactly the computation you care about. Interpretability of the found features is bought with fidelity to the actual activations
ShrinkageThe L1 penalty biases feature magnitudes toward zero, systematically distorting activationsThe direct motivation for TopK and gated variants
Evaluation is unsolved"Interpretable" is judged by human or LLM inspection of top-activating examples, which is biased toward features that look clean and is not a measure of completeness or causal correctnessWithout a solid metric, comparing SAE methods is difficult and progress claims are soft. Downstream causal metrics are an active area
Downstream performance gapsSome evaluations have found SAE-based interventions underperforming simpler baselines on practical tasksThe gap between "we found interpretable features" and "these features are the useful unit of analysis" is not closed

The open conceptual question. SAEs assume the model's computation decomposes into a sparse sum of linear directions. That assumption is imported from the superposition hypothesis, which is itself best-established in toy models. If real models use representations that are not sparse-linear in this way — nonlinear features, genuinely distributed codes, features that only exist relative to context — SAEs would still produce a dictionary that reconstructs well and looks interpretable, because a sufficiently large overcomplete dictionary can fit a lot. That is the uncomfortable possibility the gotcha below addresses.

Causal Methods: Patching, Ablation, Path Analysis

The methodological core of the field, and the thing that distinguishes it from earlier interpretability work: intervention, not correlation. A component that activates during a behavior may be causing it, may be a downstream consequence of it, or may be irrelevant. Only intervening distinguishes these.

Activation patching (also called causal tracing, or interchange intervention in the causal-abstraction literature) is the workhorse.

Build a MINIMAL PAIR of prompts differing in one relevant respect:
    clean:     "The Eiffel Tower is in the city of"  -> " Paris"
    corrupted: "The Colosseum is in the city of"     -> " Rome"

Procedure:
    1. Run clean, cache ALL internal activations.
    2. Run corrupted; note the (wrong-for-clean) output.
    3. Re-run corrupted, but at ONE chosen site (layer, position,
       head, or feature) SUBSTITUTE the cached clean activation.
    4. Measure how far the output moves back toward the clean answer.

    patching effect = metric(patched) - metric(corrupted)
                      normalized by metric(clean) - metric(corrupted)

    Sweep the site over all (layer, position) pairs -> a heatmap of
    WHERE the distinguishing information lives and moves.

Directions matter and answer different questions:
    denoising  (clean -> corrupted run): which components SUFFICE
                to restore correct behavior
    noising    (corrupted -> clean run): which components are
                NECESSARY -- breaking them breaks behavior
    Necessity and sufficiency can dissociate, e.g. under redundancy.

Path patching refines this. Ordinary patching changes a component's output everywhere downstream, so it cannot tell you which downstream consumer mattered. Path patching restricts the intervention to a specific edge — patch the contribution of head A only as it enters head B's queries, leaving A's other paths at their corrupted values. This is what turns a set of important components into an actual wiring diagram, and it is how circuits are established rather than merely localized.

Ablation replaces a component's output with a baseline. The choice of baseline is a real methodological decision, not a detail: zero-ablation pushes activations off-distribution and can produce misleading effects; mean-ablation (the average over a distribution) is the usual default; resample-ablation (a value from another input) keeps things on-distribution. Reported ablation effects are only interpretable alongside the baseline used.

The canonical worked example. Wang et al. (2022), Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 Small, applied this machinery end-to-end to a real, if small, model. The task: complete "When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to" with " Mary". They identified a circuit of around 26 heads in several functional classes — duplicate token heads, S-inhibition heads, name mover heads, and (notably) backup name mover heads that take over when the primary ones are ablated. That last finding is the important methodological warning: networks contain redundancy that makes naive ablation understate a component's role, because the network self-repairs. Any claim resting on "ablating X barely changed the output, so X does not matter" must rule out backup behavior.

Other standard tools. The logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020) applies the unembedding matrix to intermediate residual stream states to read out what the model would predict if it stopped at that layer — a cheap and revealing view of how predictions form across depth. It is unreliable in places, because intermediate representations are not in the same basis the unembedding expects. The tuned lens (Belrose et al., 2023, Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens) fixes this by learning a per-layer affine probe to map intermediate states into the final-layer basis, giving substantially better-calibrated readouts — at the cost of a trained component per layer, which introduces its own question about what the probe added (a concern taken up in section 15.2).

Automated circuit discovery. Manual circuit analysis costs months per circuit, which does not scale to a frontier model. ACDC (Conmy et al., 2023, Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability) automates the search by iteratively pruning edges from the computational graph whose removal does not degrade a task metric beyond a threshold, recovering circuits similar to hand-derived ones on tasks where ground truth exists. Attribution patching approximates patching effects with gradients, making it possible to estimate every site's effect in a couple of backward passes instead of one forward pass per site — a large constant-factor win, at the cost of a linear approximation that degrades for large interventions. These methods make circuit discovery tractable; they still require a task with clean minimal pairs and a well-defined metric, which is the binding constraint for anything resembling open-ended model behavior.

Where the Program Actually Stands

This is the part most often oversold, so it is worth stating without hedging in either direction.

Genuinely establishedPromising but unresolvedFar out of reach
Specific circuits fully reverse-engineered in small models (induction heads; IOI in GPT-2 small) with causal verificationSAEs recovering interpretable features at frontier scale, with causal steering evidenceA complete mechanistic account of any frontier model
Causal intervention methodology — patching, path patching, ablation with proper baselines — as a rigorous toolkitWhether SAE features are the right unit of analysis (13.5)Verifying the absence of a capability or disposition by inspecting weights
Superposition as a mechanism, demonstrated in toy models built to test itAutomated circuit discovery scaling beyond narrow tasks with clean metricsReading a model's goals or intentions off its internals
Polysemanticity as a ubiquitous empirical factWhether small-model findings transfer to frontier scaleCertifying a model safe on mechanistic grounds

The honest summary. Mech interp has produced real, verified, causally-established results — and they are on small models, narrow tasks, and specific circuits. The gap to "we understand what a frontier model is doing" is enormous, and it is not obviously a gap that more of the same closes: the number of circuits scales with the model, the interactions between them are not additive, and no current method verifies that a discovered circuit is the whole story rather than one path among many. Set against that, the field is genuinely young and moving fast, the tooling is far better than it was two years ago, and the SAE results represent a real step from "small models" to "frontier models."

The strongest argument for the program does not depend on completeness. Section 10.8 showed behavioral evaluation can be defeated by a model whose training-time and test-time behavior are identical by construction. Any method that inspects only inputs and outputs is defeated by exactly the failure modes that matter most. Mech interp is currently the main research direction that could, in principle, escape that — and "in principle" is doing real work in that sentence.

Gotcha The most consequential open question in this section is whether SAE features are the right unit of analysis at all, and it is easy to miss because the method's outputs are so compelling. The logic runs: superposition says features are sparse non-orthogonal directions; therefore sparse dictionary learning should recover them; the recovered features look interpretable and steering them works; therefore we have found the model's features. The weak step is the first — superposition is best-established in toy models constructed to exhibit it, and its application to real models is inference from consistent evidence, not demonstration. If a frontier model's computation is not well-described as a sparse sum of linear directions, a large overcomplete dictionary would still reconstruct activations well and still yield human-labelable features, because a sufficiently expressive basis fits nearly anything and humans are good at finding stories in top-activating examples. Feature splitting is the visible symptom: if the feature count is partly set by your dictionary size, you are not straightforwardly reading off the model's own units. Two guards. First, treat interpretability-by-inspection as generating hypotheses only — a feature earns the description "used by the model" when intervening on it changes behavior as predicted, which is why the steering results in Templeton et al. (2024) matter far more than the feature labels. Second, remember that even a perfectly recovered feature dictionary is a vocabulary, not a mechanism: knowing what is represented is not knowing what algorithm operates on it, and circuits are what supply the second part.
